How much to charge to install a sump pump

The number a homeowner wants is a published “$450 pump swap” special, or a price they saw for a replacement on a coupon site. That number is not a takeoff. A 1/3 HP swap in an existing pit with fifteen included feet of discharge is not the same job as a new basin cut through a concrete slab, a 1/2 HP pump, forty feet of discharge, a battery backup, and a high-water alarm. The trip is the same. The hours are not.

Open the free bid calculator

Count the pit and the backup, not just the pump

Basement-waterproofing calculators price interior drain tile, French drains, and crawl encapsulation. Well-pump calculators price depth, a pitless adapter, and a pressure tank. A sump install is a different job: the pump, the pit, the discharge past the included first fifteen feet, and the backup that is not in the coupon. Quoting all of that from a published swap special is how the first saw cut eats the field margin.

A job with the same trip can cost much more

Each extra foot of discharge past the included first fifteen is time that never appears on the coupon. A new pit is billed as its own hours. A concrete slab cut, a battery backup, and an alarm are adders that get forgotten on a brochure special. On the sample rates a new-slab 1/2 HP install with forty feet of discharge, a battery backup, and an alarm prices about $3,455.03 (12.2 crew-hours, walk-away $2,418.52). The same shop’s existing-pit 1/3 HP swap prices about $738.90 (2.5 hours, walk-away $517.23). Matching the brochure job’s $450 special on the slab house is how that job becomes a loss — the $450 special already loses $67.23 even on the brochure swap.

Battery backup and a dirt-crawl new pit are not automatically a markup on the swap

Adding a battery backup and an alarm to the existing-pit swap is not the $450 special plus 15%. On the sample rates that package prices about $1,644.70 (3.9 crew-hours). A new dirt-crawl 3/4 HP install with a water-powered backup, fifty feet of discharge, freeze protection, and a permit prices about $3,443.62 (11.9 hours). Treating either as a blended add-on is how the special that looked fine turns into a loss after the first basin set.

Load the wage, then keep a walk-away number

A $42/h installer loaded at 34% payroll burden is $56.28. Margin is a share of the price you send, not a markup on cost. The walk-away price is total cost — below that the job makes nothing before you take a dollar home. Replace every rate with your invoices before you send either number.

What this is not

This is not a waterproofing design, a drainage plan, a building-code determination, a permit, an engineering stamp, or a recommended market price. It is arithmetic on the numbers you type. Pump size, pit type, discharge, backup, alarm, and freeze protection are yours to confirm. It does not price a basement waterproofing system or a well-pump replacement.

Price your sump-pump install

Common questions

How much to charge to install a sump pump?

Charge from the trip, the pump swap, a new pit versus an existing-pit swap, extra discharge past the included first fifteen feet, battery or water-powered backup, alarm, freeze protection, loaded labor, overhead, and a margin that is a share of price. A default 1/3 HP existing-pit swap with fifteen included feet of discharge, at the sample rates in this calculator, prices around $739 — about 2.5 crew-hours.

Why is a $450 sump pump special dangerous?

Homeowners count a pump. Pit excavation, a concrete slab cut, extra discharge, and the backup that is often more than the primary do not scale with that number. Matching a cheaper special written for an existing-pit swap is how a new-pit-and-battery job becomes a two-day loss. On the sample rates the $450 special is already $67 under the walk-away cost of the brochure swap.

How much to charge to install a sump pump with a new pit and battery backup?

A new basin cut through a slab with a 1/2 HP pump, forty feet of discharge, a battery backup, and an alarm is not a swap special. On the sample rates that job prices around $3,455 (12.2 crew-hours, walk-away $2,419), while the existing-pit 1/3 HP swap prices around $739 (2.5 hours).

      Hand the customer a proposal

      The price above is for you. This is the page you print or save as a PDF and give to the customer — your details, their details, the scope, the deposit split, and a line for them to sign. Your business details are saved on this device so you only type them once; the customer’s details are never saved.

      Everything on the printed page is text you typed or a number this calculator worked out. It contains no warranty, lien, or cancellation wording — those depend on your jurisdiction and your contract, and this tool is not the place to invent them.

      Common questions

      Why does a two-and-a-half hour job price at $739?

      Because hours are the smallest part of it. The default swap runs 2.45 hours including a 0.85-hour trip and 0.5 hours of site time, which is $137.89 of loaded labor — but the pump and check valve add $223, travel and equipment $85, and overhead $71.34, for a $517.23 cost before margin. Labor is 26.7% of direct cost here; material is 43.1%. Short jobs are priced by what it costs to show up, not by the clock.

      Why does the trip count as billable hours?

      Because it consumes the same crew hour a wrench does. The 0.85-hour trip allowance is loaded at the same $56.28 rate as the work itself ($42 wage plus 34% burden), which is what stops a half-hour job across town from quietly costing you money. The separate travel-and-equipment line covers the vehicle rather than the person.

      Why is the discharge pipe $0 when I entered 15 feet?

      Because 15 feet is exactly the included allowance. The base price carries the first 15 ft of discharge run, so extra footage is zero and nothing bills at the $6.50 per-foot rate. Enter 30 feet and 15 of them become chargeable. The allowance is editable for the same reason as every other rate on this page — it should match how you actually bundle it.

      Does a backup pump change the answer much?

      Substantially, and it is off by default. The defaults price a primary swap only, with no battery or water-powered backup, no high-water alarm, and no freeze protection on the discharge. Those are the lines that separate a $739 swap from a system a homeowner would actually call protected, so if you are being compared against a quote that includes them, turn them on before comparing.

vs-a-flat-pump-swap-special.html.text:
← Sump Pump Bid Calculator

This calculator vs. a flat pump-swap special

“$X, any sump pump, done” is not a price for a sump-pump job — it is a price for an existing pit and the primary pump alone, quietly applied to a new basin cut through a slab with a battery backup too.

What a flat pump-swap special is

A flat swap special is the fastest way to quote a sump-pump call over the phone: name a number and go. Customers like it because it is easy to compare against a competitor's coupon, and it is the number a homeowner holding one will ask you to match.

The number behind it was usually set for the simplest version of the job — a pump that has already failed in a pit that already exists, swapped for a like-for-like replacement — and then reused for every call afterward, whether or not the next one needs a new pit cut through a slab, forty feet of discharge, or a battery backup the homeowner asks for once the tech is already there.

What this calculator is

This page keeps no account and sends nothing to a server. You pick a pump size, a pit type — existing pit, new pit in dirt, or a new pit cut through a slab — discharge footage past the included first fifteen feet, a backup (none, battery, or water-powered), whether to add an alarm or freeze protection, and your own wage, payroll burden, travel, overhead, and target margin. It prices the pit, the extra discharge, and the backup as their own lines, on top of the swap itself, and returns the price, the crew-hour split, the effective hourly rate, and the walk-away price — for this job, not a flat number for every sump pump.

What a flat swap special doesWhat this calculator does instead
Charges the same price whether the pit already exists or has to be cut through a concrete slab, even though the slab cut alone adds crew-hours and a disposal cost the swap never needed. Prices pit work by type — existing pit, new pit in dirt, or new pit through a slab — with its own hours and basin/slab-cut cost for each.
Has no line for a battery or water-powered backup, which this calculator's own suggested kit prices in parts alone at more than the primary pump. Prices backup as its own package — hours and kit cost — separate from the primary pump swap.
Bills the same for fifteen feet of discharge and forty, even though every foot past the included distance adds pipe and labor. Prices extra discharge footage past the included distance at its own per-foot hours and material rate.
Has no per-line breakdown — a slab cut, a backup, and an alarm sold together disappear into one flat number. Reports labor cost, material cost, overhead, and price as separate lines, so a shop can see exactly what a slab-and-battery job costs to run.
Gives the estimator a number to quote, not a number to check a quote against. Reports the price, the profit, and the effective hourly rate, so a shopped price can be scored against real cost before you commit to it.

The same swap special, two different jobs

Using this calculator's own suggested figures for each preset, at a 30% target margin, a $42 hourly wage, 34% payroll burden, and $85 in travel and equipment:

An existing-pit swap — a 1/3 HP pump, no backup, and discharge within the included fifteen feet — costs $517.23 to run and this calculator prices it at $738.90. The same trip, but the pit has to be cut through a concrete slab, the homeowner wants a 1/2 HP pump, the discharge run is forty feet, and they add a battery backup: that job costs $2,418.52 to run — 4.68 times the swap's cost, on the same trip and the same crew wage — and this calculator prices it at $3,455.03, still the target 30% margin. Quote the slab-and-battery job at the swap special's flat $738.90 price instead, and it prices $1,679.62 below its own break-even cost — before counting the $2,716.13 it falls short of this calculator's own price. Same swap special, one job that pays and one that loses money the moment the slab saw and the battery kit show up.

Common questions

Why does a flat pump-swap special get a new-pit job wrong?

Because the special was priced for an existing pit and the primary pump alone, and the cost drivers for a new-pit, battery-backup job are not in that price at all. Using this calculator's own suggested figures, an existing-pit 1/3 HP swap costs $517.23 to run, and a new pit cut through a slab with a 1/2 HP pump, 40 ft of discharge, and a battery backup costs $2,418.52 to run -- 4.68 times as much, on the same trip and the same crew wage.

What does a flat pump-swap special usually leave out entirely?

The pit and the backup. A pump-swap special has no line for cutting a new basin through a slab or dirt floor, no line for discharge past the first included feet, and no line for a battery or water-powered backup, which this calculator's own suggested kit prices at more than the primary pump itself. It also has no line for a high-water alarm or freeze protection, which are commonly sold alongside a backup.

How big is the pricing gap in practice?

On this calculator's own suggested figures: the existing-pit swap prices at $738.90, on a job that costs $517.23 to run, holding a 30% target margin. The new pit, 1/2 HP pump, 40 ft of discharge, and battery backup costs $2,418.52 to run, and this calculator prices it at $3,455.03, still the same 30% margin. Quoting that job at the swap special's $738.90 price leaves it $1,679.62 below its own break-even cost -- before counting the $2,716.13 shortfall against what this calculator prices the same job at.

Is a flat pump-swap special ever the right way to quote?

For a narrow band of jobs -- an existing pit, the primary pump only, no backup, and discharge within the included footage -- a flat swap special can land close, because that is probably the job the price was set on. The risk is quoting a new pit, a battery or water-powered backup, or extra discharge sight unseen, because the special does not know what is under the floor until someone opens it up, and by then the flat number has often already been quoted over the phone.

Does this calculator know my local labor rates or parts costs?

No. It has no data on your local labor market, your supplier's parts pricing, or what other plumbers in your area charge. It takes pump size, pit type, discharge footage past the included first fifteen feet, backup type, alarm, freeze protection, and your own wage, burden, travel, overhead, and target margin, and turns that into a price for this job -- the arithmetic a flat swap special skips, not a market survey.

This calculator vs. ServiceTitan

Two different shapes: ServiceTitan is an account-based field service management platform for running a plumbing company's whole operation. This page is a free, private worksheet for one question — what should this one sump-pump install cost, given its pit, its discharge, and its backup, before you quote it.

What each tool is for

ServiceTitan is a field service management platform, founded in 2007 by Ara Mahdessian and Vahe Kuzoyan, headquartered in Glendale, California. It serves HVAC, plumbing, electrical, and other trades with scheduling, dispatch, invoicing, marketing, reporting, and job costing across a whole business, with a mobile app for crews in the field. It is an account-based platform: you sign up and use it as an ongoing service across a whole company, not a one-off calculator. ServiceTitan's own pricing page is not reachable from this session to confirm today's exact plan names or dollar figures, so no price for it is invented here: only its well-documented identity and category — field service management software serving plumbing among other trades, sold as a subscription account — are stated, and no dollar amount for ServiceTitan appears on this page.

This calculator does none of what ServiceTitan does. It does not schedule techs, dispatch crews, or invoice a customer, and it stores no customer or job record on a server. It takes one sump-pump job's pump size (1/3, 1/2, or 3/4 HP), pit type (existing-pit swap, new dirt pit, or a new pit cut through a concrete slab), discharge footage past the included first fifteen feet, battery or water-powered backup, a high-water alarm, a check valve, and freeze protection, plus your crew wage, payroll burden, travel and equipment, overhead, and target margin. It turns that into the price, the crew-hour split between the swap and the pit/discharge/backup package, the price per discharge foot, the effective hourly rate, and the walk-away price below which the job loses money — plus, if you already have a price on the table, a check of whether it clears that floor. It runs free in any browser, keeps no account, and uploads nothing you type.

Common questions

Should I use this calculator or ServiceTitan?

They do different jobs, and a plumbing or basement-waterproofing shop of any size will likely end up touching both eventually. Does this calculator design the drainage or size the pump for me?

No. Hours and material rates are ballpark shop figures you can edit, not a drainage design, a horsepower sizing calculation, or a code determination. Whether a pit needs a check valve, whether local code requires a backup, and what horsepower a given basin actually needs are still a judgment call for the licensed plumber on site.
